lesson.title: Hidden Twins: Body & World
lesson.subtitle: Arm, Hand, Finger, Haus, Glas, Brot — words that crossed the sea untouched

hook.title: The Zero-Shift Zone
hook.content: Point at your hand. The word you just thought of is German. Hand is Hand, Arm is Arm, Finger is Finger — spelled identically, letter for letter, after 1,500 years on opposite shores of the North Sea. Around every such zero-shift twin, a small world of identical words gathers: Haus, Glas, Brot, Gold, Sand, Butter, Ring. You did not learn German words today. You noticed the ones you always owned.

footnotes.title: Why Untouched?
footnotes.content: These words are identical precisely because they contain none of the consonants the High German Shift touched in the positions it touched them — no initial p, t, k, or th. Arm, Hand, Finger, Ring, Haus, Glas, Brot, Gold, Sand, Butter: every consonant sat in a safe seat when the sound wave rolled through.

pattern.title: Recognize the Twin, Then Flag the Gender
pattern.content: There is no transformation to learn here — only recognition plus one new habit: German flags every noun with a gender. Arm (der), Finger (der), Ring (der), and Sand (der) are masculine; Hand (die) and Butter (die) are feminine; Haus, Glas, Brot, and Gold (das) are neuter. The flag is not logic, it is ancestry — so collect it together with the word, the way you collect pronunciation with a word in any language.

footnotes.title: Brot Is 'the Brewed Thing'
footnotes.content: Brot traces to Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally 'the fermented, risen thing', kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread and brew are branches of the same ancient root; bread was named after its foam.

footnotes.title: You Eat the Cognate Weekly
footnotes.content: A Hamburger is simply 'of Hamburg' — the city's name plus the German adjectival -er, exactly as in Berliner or Wiener. English kept the German grammar inside the sandwich.

exercises.prompt: Match each English word with its identical German twin:
exercises.explanation: Zero-shift twins: no consonant of these words sat in a shifted position, so the spellings survived side by side.

exercises.prompt: What everyday English word is the exact twin of German 'Brot'?
exercises.explanation: Brot and bread are the same Proto-Germanic word — and Brot is kin to the verb brew: bread is 'the brewed thing'.
Ring is masculine: der Ring — the exact English word, kept for the circle on a finger. Gender is ancestry, not logic — collect it with the word.

exercises.prompt: Give the capitalized German noun for the five-fingered body part at the end of your arm:
exercises.english_hint: no shift at all — just the German capital
exercises.explanation: Hand is spelled identically in both languages; German simply capitalizes all nouns.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I find the gold in the sand'
exercises.target_answer: Ich finde das Gold im Sand
exercises.meaning: I find the gold in the sand

vocab_hints.note: Gold is neuter: das Gold (Sand is masculine — der Sand)
im = in + dem, the all-purpose 'in the' for masculine and neuter places

exercises.explanation: Verb in position 2: 'Ich finde...'. 'im' is the contraction of in + dem — one tile instead of two.

summary.outcome: Recognize ten zero-shift cognate nouns and attach their gender flags.

use_example.german: Das Brot und das Gold im Haus.
use_example.english: The bread and the gold in the house.

summary.takeaway: Words without shiftable consonants crossed unchanged — and each noun carries a gender flag you collect with the word.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: You own fifteen words — that is enough for real sentences. Time to build your first six.

twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich finde das Gold im Sand" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Hidden Twins: Body & World without relying on short-term echo.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

gold.context_phrase: Nicht alles, was glänzt, ist Gold.
gold.context_translation: Not all that glitters is gold.

sand.context_translation: The children play in the sand.

butter.etymology_derivation: Borrowed together into West Germanic from Latin butyrum / Greek boutyron.

nudel.context_translation: The noodles cook for ten minutes.
nudel.etymology_derivation: Attested since the 16th century with unknown deeper origin, possibly a variant of Knödel; English noodle was borrowed from German Nudel. [wiktionary]

doppelt.etymology_derivation: Past participle of doppeln, borrowed from Old French doble — the very word that became English double. [wiktionary]

waschmaschine.context_translation: The washing machine is running in the basement.
waschmaschine.etymology_derivation: Compound of waschen and Maschine; waschen is a direct cognate of English wash, and Maschine matches English machine, both from Latin machina. [wiktionary]

wurzel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wurzala, from Proto-Germanic *wurt- plus *waluz. Old English wyrtwalu and modern English wort, as in plant names, are the cognates. [wiktionary]

stimmung.context_phrase: Die Stimmung auf der Party war super.
stimmung.context_translation: The mood at the party was great.
stimmung.etymology_derivation: stimmen (to be right, to tune) + -ung: your mood is the tuning of your inner instrument. [wiktionary]

schwimmbad.context_phrase: Das Schwimmbad ist im Sommer voll.
schwimmbad.context_translation: The swimming pool is full in summer.
schwimmbad.etymology_derivation: schwimmen + Bad — the swim-bath; both elements are documented twins (swim, bath). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
